notes: Reasoning Ability part of BATCH_006: 200 original questions (60 Basic, 80 Intermediate, 60 Advanced) built by tools/batch_006/reasoning.py. New puzzle structures and noun sets. Puzzles are brute-forced for a unique arrangement; syllogisms are checked over every Venn-region model; inequalities over all integer assignments; data sufficiency by enumerating models for each statement subset; blood relations, directions, coding (inferred rules checked against alternative simple rules), series, alphabet, number operations, ranking and input-output are recomputed in code. Verbal-reasoning items are hand-written and were re-answered blind by a separate solver. All questions await human review.

stimuli.title: Six friends at a round table, with favourite games
stimuli.content:
Six friends Anupama, Bhushan, Gulzar, Madhavi, Rajat and Tanvir sit around a circular table, equally spaced and all facing the centre. Each likes a different game among Carrom, Checkers, Chess, Ludo, Pachisi and Scrabble. (Facing the centre, a person's right is the next seat anticlockwise.)

- Rajat sits second to the right of Anupama.
- Madhavi sits immediately to the left of Rajat.
- The person who likes Chess sits opposite Anupama, and that person is Gulzar.
- Tanvir is not an immediate neighbour of Gulzar.
- The person who likes Carrom sits immediately to the right of Gulzar.
- Anupama likes Ludo and Rajat likes Scrabble.
- Madhavi does not like Pachisi.
stimuli.solution:
Step 1: Put Anupama at seat 0 and number the seats anticlockwise. Rajat = 2, Madhavi = 1 (immediately to Rajat's left), Gulzar (Chess) = 3, opposite Anupama.
Step 2: Seats 4 and 5 remain for Bhushan and Tanvir. Seat 4 is next to Gulzar, so Tanvir = 5 and Bhushan = 4.
Step 3: Carrom is immediately to Gulzar's right: seat 4, Bhushan. Anupama Ludo, Rajat Scrabble; Checkers and Pachisi remain for Madhavi and Tanvir, and Madhavi does not like Pachisi, so Madhavi Checkers and Tanvir Pachisi.

| Seat (anticlockwise) | Person | Game |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | Anupama | Ludo |
| 1 | Madhavi | Checkers |
| 2 | Rajat | Scrabble |
| 3 | Gulzar | Chess |
| 4 | Bhushan | Carrom |
| 5 | Tanvir | Pachisi |

stimuli.title: Four men and four women seated alternately
stimuli.content:
Eight persons sit around a circular table, equally spaced and all facing the centre. Four of them — Jaiwant, Mahesh, Prabal and Sudhir — are men, and the other four — Kalpita, Rupali, Swati and Vaishali — are women. (Facing the centre, a person's right is the next seat anticlockwise.)

- Men and women sit alternately.
- Sudhir sits opposite Jaiwant.
- Swati sits immediately to the right of Sudhir.
- Rupali sits second to the left of Swati.
- Prabal sits immediately to the left of Rupali.
- Vaishali is an immediate neighbour of both Mahesh and Jaiwant.
stimuli.solution:
Step 1: Put Jaiwant at seat 0 and number the seats anticlockwise. Men take the even seats and women the odd seats.
Step 2: Sudhir = 4 (opposite Jaiwant); Swati = 5 (to his right); Rupali = 3 (second to Swati's left); Prabal = 2 (immediately to Rupali's left). Mahesh takes the last man's seat, 6.
Step 3: Vaishali neighbours both Mahesh (6) and Jaiwant (0): seat 7. Kalpita = 1.

| Seat (anticlockwise) | Person |
|---|---|
| 0 | Jaiwant |
| 1 | Kalpita |
| 2 | Prabal |
| 3 | Rupali |
| 4 | Sudhir |
| 5 | Swati |
| 6 | Mahesh |
| 7 | Vaishali |

stimuli.title: A rectangular table with outward-facing end seats
stimuli.content:
Six persons Hiranya, Jasmeet, Keshava, Lopamudra, Nakul and Revati sit around a rectangular table. The longer sides of the table are to the north and south, and each has two seats; the shorter sides are to the west and east, and each has one seat. The four persons on the longer sides face the centre of the table, while the two persons at the shorter (end) sides face away from the table. Seats on the north side are directly across from the seats on the south side, and the west-end seat is directly across from the east-end seat. (Facing the centre, a person's right is the next seat anticlockwise; facing outside, it is the next seat clockwise.)

- Nakul sits at the west end of the table.
- Revati sits immediately to the right of Nakul.
- Keshava sits directly across the table from Revati.
- Jasmeet sits second to the right of Keshava.
- Lopamudra sits immediately to the left of Jasmeet.
stimuli.solution:
Going anticlockwise from the west end the seats are: west end, south-west, south-east, east end, north-east, north-west.
Step 1: Nakul (west end) faces outside, so his right is clockwise: Revati = north-west.
Step 2: Keshava is across from Revati: south-west. He faces the centre, so his right is anticlockwise: south-east, then the east end — Jasmeet.
Step 3: Jasmeet faces outside, so her left is anticlockwise: Lopamudra = north-east. Hiranya takes the last seat, south-east.

| Seat | Person | Facing |
|---|---|---|
| west end | Nakul | outside |
| south side, west seat | Keshava | centre |
| south side, east seat | Hiranya | centre |
| east end | Jasmeet | outside |
| north side, east seat | Lopamudra | centre |
| north side, west seat | Revati | centre |

stimuli.title: Twelve chairs around a square table, two vacant
stimuli.content:
A square table has three chairs along each side — one at each end of the side and one in the middle — so there are twelve chairs, equally spaced around the table. Going round the table, the last chair of one side is next to the first chair of the next side. Ten persons Anvita, Bhargav, Chaitra, Haridas, Indumati, Kumud, Laxman, Mandakini, Nachiket and Parimal sit on ten of the chairs, all facing the centre, and two chairs are vacant. (Facing the centre, a person's right is the next chair anticlockwise. Vacant chairs are counted as chairs.)

- Anvita sits in the middle chair of a side, and Kumud sits directly opposite her (in the middle chair of the opposite side).
- Laxman sits third to the right of Kumud.
- Chaitra sits second to the right of Anvita, and Nachiket sits immediately to the right of Anvita.
- The two vacant chairs are on the same side of the table; it is neither Anvita's side nor Kumud's side.
- Bhargav sits immediately to the left of a vacant chair.
- Haridas sits on the same side as Kumud, but not in the middle chair, and Mandakini sits immediately to the left of Haridas.
- Indumati sits in the middle chair of a side.
stimuli.solution:
Number the chairs 0 to 11 anticlockwise so that Anvita is in chair 1, the middle of side A (chairs 0–2); side B has chairs 3–5, side C 6–8 and side D 9–11.
Step 1: Kumud = 7 (middle of side C). Laxman = 7 + 3 = 10. Nachiket = 2, Chaitra = 3.
Step 2: The vacant chairs share a side other than A and C. On side B, chair 3 is Chaitra's, so the vacant chairs would be 4 and 5; then Bhargav would have to be in chair 3 or 4 — impossible. So the vacant chairs are on side D: 9 and 11 (Laxman has 10), and Bhargav = 8 (immediately to the left of chair 9).
Step 3: Haridas is on side C but not in the middle; chair 8 is Bhargav's, so Haridas = 6 and Mandakini = 5. Indumati takes the middle chair 4, and Parimal the last chair, 0.

| Side | Chairs (anticlockwise) |
|---|---|
| A | Parimal, Anvita, Nachiket |
| B | Chaitra, Indumati, Mandakini |
| C | Haridas, Kumud, Bhargav |
| D | vacant, Laxman, vacant |

stimuli.title: Six floors and six curtain colours
stimuli.content:
Six persons Bhanu, Chandana, Girish, Purab, Ujjwal and Vasanti live on the six floors of a building, one on each floor. Floor 1 is the lowermost and floor 6 the topmost. Each has curtains of a different colour among Beige, Maroon, Mauve, Teal, Turquoise and Violet.

- Purab lives on floor 4, and Chandana lives immediately below Purab.
- Vasanti lives on the topmost floor.
- Only one person lives between Bhanu and Chandana.
- Girish lives on an odd-numbered floor.
- Ujjwal lives on a floor below Bhanu's floor.
- Bhanu has Teal curtains, and the person with Maroon curtains lives immediately above him.
- Girish has Beige curtains, and the person with Mauve curtains lives immediately above Girish.
- Chandana has neither Violet nor Mauve curtains.
stimuli.solution:
Step 1: Purab = 4, Chandana = 3, Vasanti = 6. Bhanu is two floors from Chandana: floor 1 or 5.
Step 2: Ujjwal lives below Bhanu, so Bhanu cannot be on floor 1: Bhanu = 5. Floors 1 and 2 remain for Girish and Ujjwal; Girish is on an odd floor, so Girish = 1 and Ujjwal = 2.
Step 3: Bhanu Teal ⇒ Maroon on floor 6 (Vasanti). Girish Beige ⇒ Mauve on floor 2 (Ujjwal). Turquoise and Violet remain for Chandana and Purab; Chandana is not Violet, so Chandana Turquoise and Purab Violet.

| Floor | Person | Curtains |
|---|---|---|
| 6 | Vasanti | Maroon |
| 5 | Bhanu | Teal |
| 4 | Purab | Violet |
| 3 | Chandana | Turquoise |
| 2 | Ujjwal | Mauve |
| 1 | Girish | Beige |

stimuli.title: Seven floors and their potted plants
stimuli.content:
Seven persons Abhijit, Deepali, Faiyaz, Kamakshi, Leeladhar, Ojaswini and Rishi live on the seven floors of a building, one on each floor (floor 1 is the lowermost, floor 7 the topmost). Each keeps a different number of potted plants among 4, 6, 7, 9, 12, 15 and 18.

- The person who keeps 18 plants lives on floor 5, and Kamakshi lives two floors below that person.
- Kamakshi keeps exactly half as many plants as the person who lives immediately above her.
- The person who keeps 15 plants lives immediately below Kamakshi.
- Rishi lives on the topmost floor and keeps fewer plants than Kamakshi.
- Only two persons live between Rishi and Faiyaz.
- Abhijit lives on a floor above Faiyaz's floor and keeps the second-smallest number of plants.
- Deepali keeps an odd number of plants, and Leeladhar keeps fewer plants than Deepali.
stimuli.solution:
Step 1: 18 plants on floor 5; Kamakshi = 3; 15 plants on floor 2.
Step 2: Kamakshi's count doubled must be on floor 4. Possible pairs from the list: 6 and 12, or 9 and 18 — but 18 is on floor 5, so Kamakshi keeps 6 and floor 4 has 12.
Step 3: Rishi = 7 with fewer than 6 plants: 4. Faiyaz is three floors below Rishi: floor 4 (12 plants).
Step 4: Abhijit is above Faiyaz with 7 plants; floor 5 has 18, so Abhijit = 6. Floor 1 then has 9 plants.
Step 5: Deepali, Leeladhar and Ojaswini take floors 1 (9), 2 (15) and 5 (18). Deepali's count is odd (9 or 15) and Leeladhar has fewer than Deepali: if Deepali had 9, nobody left would have fewer, so Deepali = floor 2 (15), Leeladhar = floor 1 (9) and Ojaswini = floor 5 (18).

| Floor | Person | Plants |
|---|---|---|
| 7 | Rishi | 4 |
| 6 | Abhijit | 7 |
| 5 | Ojaswini | 18 |
| 4 | Faiyaz | 12 |
| 3 | Kamakshi | 6 |
| 2 | Deepali | 15 |
| 1 | Leeladhar | 9 |

stimuli.title: Seven floors, three professions, no two alike adjacent
stimuli.content:
Seven persons Gobind, Harleen, Jayanti, Madhur, Nirupama, Oorja and Shailesh live on the seven floors of a building, one on each floor (floor 1 is the lowermost, floor 7 the topmost). Each of them is a Doctor, a Lawyer or a Teacher.

- Three of them are Doctors, two are Lawyers and two are Teachers.
- No two persons of the same profession live on adjacent floors.
- Madhur is a Teacher and lives on floor 4.
- Oorja is a Doctor and lives on the topmost floor.
- Harleen lives immediately below Madhur and is not a Doctor.
- Gobind lives on floor 1 and has the same profession as Oorja.
- Jayanti is a Lawyer.
- Shailesh lives on a floor below Nirupama's floor.
stimuli.solution:
Step 1: Madhur (Teacher) = 4, Oorja (Doctor) = 7, Gobind (Doctor) = 1, Harleen = 3. Harleen is not a Doctor, and as Madhur's neighbour cannot be a Teacher: Harleen is a Lawyer.
Step 2: Floor 2 lies between a Doctor (1) and a Lawyer (3), so it is a Teacher. The professions left are one Doctor and one Lawyer for floors 5 and 6; floor 6 is next to Oorja (Doctor), so floor 6 is the Lawyer and floor 5 the Doctor.
Step 3: Jayanti is a Lawyer, so she is on floor 6. Shailesh is below Nirupama, so Shailesh = 2 (Teacher) and Nirupama = 5 (Doctor).

| Floor | Person | Profession |
|---|---|---|
| 7 | Oorja | Doctor |
| 6 | Jayanti | Lawyer |
| 5 | Nirupama | Doctor |
| 4 | Madhur | Teacher |
| 3 | Harleen | Lawyer |
| 2 | Shailesh | Teacher |
| 1 | Gobind | Doctor |

stimuli.title: Four floors with three flats each, three vacant
stimuli.content:
A four-storey building (floor 1 is the lowermost, floor 4 the topmost) has three flats on each floor: West, Middle and East. Each flat is directly above the flat of the same name on the floor below. Nine persons Ajeet, Bansi, Champa, Dilip, Fulmani, Gokul, Hemangini, Indraneel and Jagjit live in nine of the twelve flats, one person per flat, and the other three flats are vacant.

- Exactly three flats are vacant, and no two vacant flats are on the same floor.
- Gokul lives in the Middle flat of floor 3, and the flat directly below his flat is vacant.
- Ajeet lives directly above Gokul, and the East flat of Ajeet's floor is vacant.
- Bansi lives in a West flat on an even-numbered floor, and Dilip lives on the same floor as Bansi.
- Hemangini lives directly below Bansi, and Fulmani lives directly above Bansi.
- Champa lives directly above Dilip.
- Jagjit lives on the same floor as Hemangini, in the East flat.
stimuli.solution:
Step 1: Gokul = 3-Middle, 2-Middle vacant; Ajeet = 4-Middle, 4-East vacant. Floors 2 and 4 now have their vacant flat, so the third vacant flat is on floor 1 or 3.
Step 2: Bansi is in a West flat on floor 2 or 4. If Bansi were in 4-West, Fulmani would have to be above floor 4 — impossible. So Bansi = 2-West, Hemangini = 1-West, Fulmani = 3-West. Dilip is on floor 2: 2-East (2-Middle is vacant). Champa = 3-East, above Dilip.
Step 3: Jagjit = 1-East. Floor 3 is now full, so the third vacant flat is on floor 1: 1-Middle. Indraneel takes the last flat, 4-West.

| Floor | West | Middle | East |
|---|---|---|---|
| 4 | Indraneel | Ajeet | vacant |
| 3 | Fulmani | Gokul | Champa |
| 2 | Bansi | vacant | Dilip |
| 1 | Hemangini | vacant | Jagjit |

stimuli.title: Ten floors, seven residents, three vacant floors
stimuli.content:
A building has ten floors, numbered 1 (lowermost) to 10 (topmost). Seven persons Ketki, Murari, Navneet, Padmini, Rehaan, Sevanti and Trilok live in it, one person per floor, so exactly three floors are vacant.

- The lowermost and topmost floors are both occupied.
- Trilok lives on floor 7, and Murari lives immediately below Trilok.
- Ketki lives below Trilok; of the floors between Ketki and Trilok, exactly two are vacant and exactly one is occupied.
- Sevanti lives on an odd-numbered floor below Ketki's floor.
- Padmini lives immediately above Trilok.
- Only one person lives above Navneet.
stimuli.solution:
Step 1: Trilok = 7, Murari = 6, Padmini = 8.
Step 2: Between Ketki and Trilok there are exactly three floors (two vacant, one occupied), so Ketki = 3. Murari (6) is the occupied one, so floors 4 and 5 are vacant.
Step 3: Sevanti is on an odd floor below 3: floor 1. That leaves one more vacant floor among 2, 9 and 10, with Navneet and Rehaan to place; floor 10 is occupied.
Step 4: Only one person lives above Navneet. If Navneet were on floor 2, many would be above him; so Navneet = 9, Rehaan = 10, and floor 2 is vacant.

| Floor | Resident |
|---|---|
| 10 | Rehaan |
| 9 | Navneet |
| 8 | Padmini |
| 7 | Trilok |
| 6 | Murari |
| 5 | vacant |
| 4 | vacant |
| 3 | Ketki |
| 2 | vacant |
| 1 | Sevanti |

stimuli.title: Six saplings planted from June to November
stimuli.content:
Six persons Anokhi, Girdhar, Kanishka, Maitreyi, Pankaj and Suhani each plant one sapling in the same year, one person in each month from June to November. Each plants a different tree among Ashoka, Banyan, Jamun, Mango, Neem and Peepal.

- Kanishka plants in the last of the six months, and she plants the Ashoka.
- Girdhar plants in a month that has 30 days.
- Pankaj plants before Girdhar, and only two persons plant between them.
- The Neem sapling is planted in June.
- Anokhi plants in the month immediately after Pankaj's month, and she plants the Mango.
- Maitreyi plants in a month after Suhani's month.
- The Banyan is planted in the month immediately before the Ashoka.
- Suhani does not plant the Peepal.
stimuli.solution:
Step 1: Kanishka = November (Ashoka). Girdhar's month has 30 days: June, September or November; Pankaj is three months before him, so Girdhar = September and Pankaj = June (Neem).
Step 2: Anokhi = July (Mango). August and October remain for Suhani and Maitreyi; Maitreyi is later, so Suhani = August and Maitreyi = October.
Step 3: Banyan is immediately before Ashoka (November): October, Maitreyi. Jamun and Peepal remain for Suhani and Girdhar; Suhani is not Peepal, so Suhani Jamun and Girdhar Peepal.

| Month | Person | Tree |
|---|---|---|
| June | Pankaj | Neem |
| July | Anokhi | Mango |
| August | Suhani | Jamun |
| September | Girdhar | Peepal |
| October | Maitreyi | Banyan |
| November | Kanishka | Ashoka |

stimuli.title: Six birth years, six birth months, ages on 1 June 2026
stimuli.content:
Six persons Avantika, Dinkar, Gurpreet, Mallika, Naresh and Shobhit were born in six different years among 1981, 1986, 1992, 1995, 1999 and 2004, and in six different months among January, March, May, July, September and November (one year and one month each). Ages are counted in completed years as on 1 June 2026: a person whose birthday month is later in the year than June has not yet had a 2026 birthday on that date.

- The person born in 1992 was born in March.
- Gurpreet is the youngest of the six and was born in January.
- Dinkar is the oldest of the six.
- As on 1 June 2026, Mallika is 30 years old and Avantika is 34 years old (in completed years).
- Naresh was born in May, and he is younger than Mallika.
- Shobhit was born in July, in a year before Avantika's year.
- Mallika was born in the latest of the six months.
stimuli.solution:
Step 1: Gurpreet = January 2004 (youngest); Dinkar = 1981 (oldest).
Step 2: Avantika is 34 on 1 June 2026: born in 1992 with a birthday by June, or in 1991 with a later birthday — 1991 is not in the list, so Avantika = 1992, and the 1992-born person was born in March: Avantika = March 1992.
Step 3: Mallika is 30: 1996 with an early birthday (not in the list) or 1995 with a birthday after June. So Mallika = 1995, and she has the latest month, November.
Step 4: Shobhit = July, in a year before 1992: 1986 (1981 is Dinkar's). Naresh = May, younger than Mallika: 1999. Dinkar takes the last month, September.

| Person | Year | Month | Age on 1 June 2026 |
|---|---|---|---|
| Dinkar | 1981 | September | 44 |
| Shobhit | 1986 | July | 39 |
| Avantika | 1992 | March | 34 |
| Mallika | 1995 | November | 30 |
| Naresh | 1999 | May | 27 |
| Gurpreet | 2004 | January | 22 |

stimuli.title: Six visits on the weekends of August 2026
stimuli.content:
A heritage museum is open to visitors only on Saturdays and Sundays. Six persons Aparna, Gajendra, Kaushiki, Manohar, Riddhima and Tejpal each visit it once in August 2026, on six different dates. 1 August 2026 is a Saturday.

- Kaushiki visits on the third Saturday of the month, and Gajendra visits on the day after Kaushiki.
- Riddhima visits on the last Saturday of the month.
- Tejpal visits exactly one week after Gajendra.
- Aparna visits exactly two weeks before Kaushiki.
- Manohar visits on a Sunday before Kaushiki, but not on the same weekend as Aparna.
stimuli.solution:
Step 1: The Saturdays are 1, 8, 15, 22 and 29 August and the Sundays 2, 9, 16, 23 and 30 August.
Step 2: Kaushiki = 15 (third Saturday), Gajendra = 16, Tejpal = 23, Riddhima = 29 (last Saturday), Aparna = 15 − 14 = 1.
Step 3: Manohar visits on a Sunday before the 15th: the 2nd or the 9th. The 2nd is on Aparna's weekend (1–2 August), so Manohar = 9.

| Date | Day | Visitor |
|---|---|---|
| 1 August | Saturday | Aparna |
| 9 August | Sunday | Manohar |
| 15 August | Saturday | Kaushiki |
| 16 August | Sunday | Gajendra |
| 23 August | Sunday | Tejpal |
| 29 August | Saturday | Riddhima |

stimuli.title: Eight meetings in morning and afternoon slots
stimuli.content:
A branch manager holds two meetings a day — one in the morning and one in the afternoon — from Monday to Thursday of a week, so there are eight meeting slots. Eight customers Aalok, Bhupesh, Daya, Hemraj, Kanika, Mohsin, Rewa and Tarini each have one meeting, in different slots. (Monday morning is the first slot and Thursday afternoon the last; slots are counted in this order.)

- Hemraj's meeting is on Wednesday afternoon.
- Aalok meets before Hemraj, and only one meeting is held between their meetings.
- Kanika meets on the same day as Aalok.
- Mohsin's meeting is the last of the week, and Bhupesh meets on the same day as Mohsin.
- Tarini meets in a morning slot on a day after Kanika's day.
- Rewa meets in an afternoon slot.
stimuli.solution:
Number the slots 1 (Monday morning) to 8 (Thursday afternoon).
Step 1: Hemraj = 6 (Wednesday afternoon). Aalok = 4 (Tuesday afternoon), so Kanika = 3 (Tuesday morning).
Step 2: Mohsin = 8 and Bhupesh = 7 (Thursday morning).
Step 3: Tarini has a morning slot on a day after Tuesday: Wednesday morning (5), as Thursday morning is taken.
Step 4: Slots 1 and 2 remain; Rewa takes the afternoon slot (2) and Daya slot 1.

| Day | Morning | Afternoon |
|---|---|---|
| Monday | Daya | Rewa |
| Tuesday | Kanika | Aalok |
| Wednesday | Tarini | Hemraj |
| Thursday | Bhupesh | Mohsin |

stimuli.title: Six insurance employees: posts and joining years
stimuli.content:
Six employees Ashwath, Deeksha, Faraaz, Ishika, Tushita and Yashwant of an insurance company hold six different posts. In decreasing order of seniority the posts are: Zonal Head, Regional Head, Branch Head, Sales Manager, Agent Supervisor and Agent Trainee. Each joined the company in a different year among 2009, 2012, 2014, 2017, 2020 and 2023. Seniority of post does not depend on the year of joining.

- Ishika is senior to all the others, and the person who joined in 2009 is immediately junior to her.
- Faraaz joined the earliest of all.
- Deeksha is the most junior, and she joined six years after Ashwath.
- Ashwath is immediately senior to Tushita, who joined in the latest year.
- Yashwant joined in 2017, five years after Ishika, and he is senior to Ashwath.
stimuli.solution:
Step 1: Ishika = Zonal Head. Faraaz joined in 2009, so he is immediately junior to her: Regional Head. Deeksha = Agent Trainee.
Step 2: Tushita joined in 2023, Yashwant in 2017 and Ishika in 2012. The years left are 2014 and 2020 for Ashwath and Deeksha, six years apart: Ashwath 2014, Deeksha 2020.
Step 3: Branch Head, Sales Manager and Agent Supervisor remain for Ashwath, Tushita and Yashwant, with Ashwath immediately above Tushita and Yashwant above Ashwath: Yashwant Branch Head, Ashwath Sales Manager, Tushita Agent Supervisor.

| Post | Employee | Joined |
|---|---|---|
| Zonal Head | Ishika | 2012 |
| Regional Head | Faraaz | 2009 |
| Branch Head | Yashwant | 2017 |
| Sales Manager | Ashwath | 2014 |
| Agent Supervisor | Tushita | 2023 |
| Agent Trainee | Deeksha | 2020 |

stimuli.title: Five two-letter code words for comparisons
stimuli.content:
In the questions of this set, the words zu, mi, ro, te and fa are used between two letters with these meanings:
'A zu B' means 'A is neither smaller than nor equal to B'; 'A mi B' means 'A is neither greater than nor equal to B'; 'A ro B' means 'A is neither greater than nor smaller than B'; 'A te B' means 'A is not smaller than B'; 'A fa B' means 'A is not greater than B'.
Assuming the statements to be true, find which of the conclusions I and II is/are definitely true.
stimuli.solution: Decode: zu means >, mi means <, ro means =, te means ≥ and fa means ≤ ('not smaller than' allows greater or equal; 'not greater than' allows smaller or equal). Rewrite each statement with ordinary signs, join them into one chain, and test each conclusion along the chain.

stimuli.title: Two-letter code words for relations
stimuli.solution: Decode each expression pair by pair from left to right, draw the small family tree it describes, and then read the asked relation off the tree. Genders come from the words used: mother, daughter and sister are female; brother and husband are male.

stimuli.title: Three coded sentences about a city
stimuli.content:
In a certain code language:
'clean the city' is written as 'ka mo ri',
'the city sleeps' is written as 'mo ri ze', and
'city lights glow' is written as 'ri pu lo'.
(The codes of the words in a sentence may be in any order.)
stimuli.solution: 'city' is the only word in all three sentences, and 'ri' the only code in all three: city = ri. Sentences 1 and 2 share 'the city' and the codes 'mo ri', so the = mo. The leftovers give clean = ka and sleeps = ze. In sentence 3, 'lights' and 'glow' share the codes 'pu' and 'lo', and nothing tells which is which.

stimuli.title: A two-step code: position shifts, then reversal for vowel-initial words
stimuli.content:
In a certain code language, every word is coded in two steps.
Step 1: Each letter in an odd position of the word (1st, 3rd, 5th, …) is replaced by the letter two places after it in the English alphabet, and each letter in an even position (2nd, 4th, …) by the letter one place before it. The alphabet wraps round (Y → A, Z → B, A → Z).
Step 2: If the word begins with a vowel, the letters obtained in step 1 are written in reverse order; otherwise they are kept in the same order.
stimuli.solution: Work letter by letter: +2 for the 1st, 3rd, 5th, … letters and −1 for the 2nd, 4th, … letters, wrapping round the alphabet. Then reverse the result only if the original word starts with A, E, I, O or U. To decode, undo step 2 first (reverse if the word might start with a vowel) and then shift back.

stimuli.title: Arrangement of 24 elements ending in a symbol
stimuli.content:
Study the following arrangement of letters, numbers and symbols and answer the question.

D 3 * K 8 L ! 6 P 2 U # 7 Q ◆ A 4 Z 9 @ G 1 Y ^
stimuli.solution: Number the elements 1 to 24 from the left. For neighbour questions, check each element's left and right neighbours; for position questions, convert right-end positions with (25 − k).

stimuli.title: Arrangement of 24 elements starting with a number
stimuli.content:
Study the following arrangement of letters, numbers and symbols and answer the question.

7 B & N 2 O 5 % H J 8 ▲ E 3 T # 9 C I 6 $ W 4 X

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Six persons Darpana, Jishnu, Kalyan, Mrinalini, Sohan and Tvisha stand in a single queue at a ticket counter, one behind another, all facing the counter.
- Kalyan stands third from the front of the queue.
- Only one person stands between Kalyan and Tvisha, and Tvisha stands behind Kalyan.
- Jishnu stands immediately in front of Tvisha.
- Darpana stands immediately in front of Kalyan.
- Sohan does not stand at the front of the queue.

How many persons stand between Mrinalini and Jishnu?

solution.concept: A queue is a row: count positions from the front
solution.explanation: Kalyan is 3rd and Tvisha 5th; Jishnu is 4th and Darpana 2nd. Positions 1 and 6 remain for Mrinalini and Sohan; Sohan is not at the front, so Mrinalini is 1st and Sohan 6th. Between Mrinalini (1st) and Jishnu (4th) stand Darpana and Kalyan: two persons.
steps: Kalyan 3, Tvisha 5, Jishnu 4, Darpana 2
Sohan not 1st ⇒ Mrinalini 1, Sohan 6
Between 1 and 4: positions 2, 3 ⇒ two
solution.why_others_wrong: One and Three miscount the positions between 1st and 4th; Four counts Mrinalini and Jishnu too.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Five persons Gautami, Hriday, Ojasvi, Pulkit and Upasana sit in a straight row, all facing south. Each owns a different vehicle among Bicycle, Car, Jeep, Scooter and Tractor. (Facing south, a person's right is towards the west and the left towards the east.)
- Ojasvi sits at the west end of the row.
- Upasana sits second to the left of Ojasvi and owns the Jeep.
- Hriday sits immediately to the right of Upasana.
- Pulkit owns the Car and sits at an extreme end of the row.
- The person who owns the Scooter sits immediately to the left of the person who owns the Tractor.

Who owns the Bicycle?

solution.concept: Facing south reverses left and right
solution.explanation: Number the seats 1 to 5 from the west. Ojasvi = 1. Facing south, the left is east, so Upasana (Jeep) = 3, and Hriday, immediately to her right (west), = 2. Pulkit (Car) is at an end: seat 5, so Gautami = 4. The Scooter owner is immediately to the left (east) of the Tractor owner; among seats 1, 2 and 4 the only adjacent pair is 1–2, so the Tractor owner is Ojasvi (1) and the Scooter owner Hriday (2), leaving the Bicycle for Gautami.
steps: Ojasvi 1; Upasana 3 (Jeep); Hriday 2
Pulkit 5 (Car) ⇒ Gautami 4
Scooter immediately east of Tractor ⇒ Ojasvi Tractor, Hriday Scooter
Gautami ⇒ Bicycle
solution.why_others_wrong: Hriday owns the Scooter, Ojasvi the Tractor and Upasana the Jeep.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Eight persons Arundhati, Bikram, Damayanti, Ganesh, Kartikeya, Niharika, Shreyas and Vaidehi sit in a straight row. Some face north and the others face south, and any two immediate neighbours face opposite directions. (Facing north, the right is east; facing south, the right is west.)
- Ganesh sits third from the west end and faces south.
- Niharika sits second to the right of Ganesh.
- Shreyas sits third to the left of Niharika.
- Vaidehi sits at an extreme end of the row and faces north.
- Bikram sits immediately to the left of Vaidehi.
- Kartikeya is not an immediate neighbour of Shreyas.
- Arundhati faces the same direction as Ganesh, and Damayanti sits somewhere to the east of Arundhati.

Who sits second to the left of Arundhati?

solution.concept: Alternating facing: one person's facing fixes everyone's
solution.explanation: Number the seats 1 to 8 from the west. Ganesh (seat 3) faces south, so every odd seat faces south and every even seat north. Niharika is second to Ganesh's right (west): seat 1, facing south; Shreyas is third to her left (east): seat 4. Vaidehi faces north from an end, so she is at seat 8; Bikram, immediately to her left (west), is at 7. Seats 2, 5 and 6 remain. Arundhati faces south, so she is at 5; Kartikeya cannot sit next to Shreyas, so he is at 2, and Damayanti at 6 (east of Arundhati). Arundhati faces south, so her left is east: seat 6, then seat 7 — Bikram.
steps: Ganesh 3 (S) ⇒ odd seats face south, even seats north
Niharika 1, Shreyas 4
Vaidehi 8 (N), Bikram 7
Arundhati 5 (odd), Kartikeya 2, Damayanti 6
Arundhati faces south ⇒ left = east ⇒ seat 7 = Bikram
solution.why_others_wrong: Ganesh is second to her right (west); Damayanti is immediately to her left; Vaidehi is third to her left.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Some persons sit in a straight row, all facing south. The number of persons is not given. (Facing south, a person's right is towards the west.)
- Mitali sits eighth from the east end of the row.
- Pranay sits fifth to the right of Mitali.
- Exactly as many persons sit to the right of Pranay as sit between Pranay and Mitali.

If Sushant sits exactly in the middle of the row, how many persons sit between Sushant and Pranay?

solution.concept: Facing south: 'to the right' means towards the west end
solution.explanation: Count positions from the west end. Pranay is five places west of Mitali, so four persons sit between them; therefore four persons sit to Pranay's right (west), making Pranay 5th from the west and Mitali 10th from the west. Mitali is 8th from the east, so the row has 10 + 8 − 1 = 17 persons and the middle seat is the 9th. Between the 5th (Pranay) and 9th (Sushant) sit three persons.
steps: Between Pranay and Mitali: 4 ⇒ 4 persons west of Pranay ⇒ Pranay 5th from west
Mitali = 5 + 5 = 10th from west
Total = 10 + 8 − 1 = 17 ⇒ middle = 9th
Between 5th and 9th: three
solution.why_others_wrong: Two and Four come from an off-by-one count of the total or of the middle seat; Five results from taking 'right' as east for a south-facing row.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Nine students Bhairavi, Chetak, Dhanush, Hamsini, Jahnavi, Kshama, Pratyush, Ruhani and Yatindra sit in a hall in three rows of three seats each — a front row, a middle row and a back row — all facing north towards the stage. The seats of each row are directly behind the seats of the row in front. (Facing north, a person's right is east; 'directly behind' means in the same column, one row further back.)
- Kshama sits in the middle seat of the middle row.
- Pratyush sits directly behind Kshama.
- Ruhani sits immediately to the left of Pratyush.
- Chetak sits at one end of the front row, and Bhairavi sits directly behind Chetak.
- Hamsini sits in the same column as Ruhani but not in the same row as Bhairavi.
- Dhanush sits in the front row.
- Yatindra does not sit in the same column as Chetak.

Who sits directly in front of the person who sits immediately to the left of Jahnavi?

solution.concept: Rows and columns: fix the grid one column at a time
solution.explanation: Kshama is in the centre seat; Pratyush is behind her (back row, middle) and Ruhani to his left (back row, west). Hamsini is in Ruhani's column (west) but not in Bhairavi's row. Bhairavi sits in the middle row (directly behind Chetak, who is in the front row), so Hamsini takes the front-row west seat. Chetak is then at the east end of the front row and Bhairavi behind him (middle row, east). Dhanush takes the front-row middle seat. Yatindra cannot be in Chetak's (east) column, so he sits in the middle row, west, and Jahnavi in the back row, east. Immediately to Jahnavi's left is Pratyush, and directly in front of Pratyush is Kshama.
steps: Kshama (middle, centre); Pratyush (back, centre); Ruhani (back, west)
Bhairavi is in the middle row ⇒ Hamsini (front, west)
Chetak (front, east), Bhairavi (middle, east)
Dhanush (front, centre); Yatindra (middle, west); Jahnavi (back, east)
Left of Jahnavi = Pratyush ⇒ in front of him = Kshama
solution.why_others_wrong: Bhairavi sits directly in front of Jahnavi herself; Dhanush is two rows in front of Pratyush; Yatindra is in front of Ruhani.

- The box at the top weighs 4 kg less than box V.

solution.explanation: The top box weighs 20 − 4 = 16 kg. F weighs half as much as the bottom box; J is the 8-kg box, so F = 12 kg and the bottom box weighs 24 kg (F itself is not at the bottom). F, R (30 kg) and J (8 kg) are consecutive from the bottom up. J cannot be at 6 (the top box weighs 16 kg), and if F were at 3, J would be at 5 and N, two places from J, would need position 3 or 7 — impossible. So F = 2, R = 3, J = 4, and N = 6 (16 kg). V (20 kg) = 5, and Z is the 24-kg box at the bottom. Above J: V (20) + N (16) = 36 kg.
steps: Top box = 16 kg; V = 20 kg below the top
F = 12 with 24 kg at the bottom ⇒ F 2, R 3, J 4, Z 1 (24)
Above J: 20 + 16 = 36 kg
solution.why_others_wrong: 44 kg adds R instead of N; 50 kg adds R and V; 28 kg adds J's own weight to V.

G is wooden: position 5 would sit on wooden K, so G = 2, which forces Q (3) to be plastic. C is above G and plastic, so C is at 5 or 8. Position 5 sits on wooden K, so it must be plastic anyway; the wooden boxes so far are G and K, and two more are needed among positions 6, 7 and 8 without two in a row — that means 6 and 8 are wooden and 7 plastic. So T (6) is wooden, C = 5 (plastic) and B = 8 (wooden).

G wooden cannot be at 5 ⇒ G = 2, Q plastic

P vs U, T vs Q, Q vs U: across the turn ⇒ undetermined
solution.why_others_wrong: Each of the other three relations crosses the turn at R = S, so it is possible but not certain — and therefore not definitely false.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: Which pair of signs, filled in order in the blanks of the expression 'G _ H ≥ J _ K = L', makes both 'G > J' and 'L ≤ J' definitely true?

solution.concept: Fill the blanks, then test both conclusions
solution.explanation: G > J needs every sign from G to J to point the same way with at least one strict sign: the first blank must be '>' (with '≥' after H). L ≤ J needs J ≥ K = L, so the second blank must be '≥', '>' or '='. Only '> and ≥' meets both: G > H ≥ J ≥ K = L. With '≥ and <', G ≥ J only and J < L; with '= and >', G ≥ J only; with '< and ≥', G and J are unrelated.
steps: G > J ⇒ first blank '>'
L ≤ J ⇒ second blank '≥', '>' or '='
Only option: > and ≥
solution.why_others_wrong: '≥ and <' and '= and >' leave G ≥ J without a strict sign; '< and ≥' reverses the direction between G and H.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Statement: V > W ≥ X; X = Y; Y < Z ≤ A

Conclusions:
I. V > Y
II. A > X
III. W ≥ Z

options.text: Only I and II are true
Only I and III are true
Only II and III are true
All I, II and III are true

solution.concept: Three conclusions: test each along the chain
solution.explanation: Combined: V > W ≥ X = Y < Z ≤ A. V > Y (I) and A ≥ Z > Y = X, i.e. A > X (II), follow. W and Z lie on opposite sides of the turn at X = Y, so W ≥ Z is not certain (III).
steps: Chain: V > W ≥ X = Y < Z ≤ A
I: V > Y ✓
II: A ≥ Z > Y = X ⇒ A > X ✓
III: across the turn ✗
solution.why_others_wrong: Every other option includes III, which compares W and Z across the turn at X = Y.
solution.final_answer: Option A: Only I and II are true

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Statement: C ≥ D; D > E; F ≤ E

Which of the following statements, if added to the given statements, makes 'G > F' definitely true?

solution.concept: The added link must join G to the chain on the correct side
solution.explanation: Combined: C ≥ D > E ≥ F. Adding G ≥ D gives G ≥ D > E ≥ F, so G > F. G = F makes G > F false; G ≤ C and G < E place G above or below a term without fixing its position relative to F.
steps: Chain: C ≥ D > E ≥ F
G ≥ D ⇒ G ≥ D > E ≥ F ⇒ G > F ✓
G = F ⇒ G > F false
G ≤ C, G < E ⇒ G could be below or above F
solution.why_others_wrong: G = F contradicts the conclusion; with G ≤ C or G < E, G may still be less than F.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Here 'A zu B' means 'A is neither smaller than nor equal to B', 'A mi B' means 'A is neither greater than nor equal to B', 'A ro B' means 'A is neither greater than nor smaller than B', 'A te B' means 'A is not smaller than B' and 'A fa B' means 'A is not greater than B'.

Statements: H te K, K ro N, N zu Q, R fa Q, R zu S, T te H

Conclusions:
I. T zu R
II. S mi K

options.text: Neither conclusion I nor II is true
Both conclusions I and II are true

solution.concept: Decoding word codes, then reading the chain
solution.explanation: Decoded: T ≥ H ≥ K = N > Q ≥ R > S. T > R (I) and S < K (II) both follow along one direction.
steps: Decode: H ≥ K, K = N, N > Q, R ≤ Q, R > S, T ≥ H
Chain: T ≥ H ≥ K = N > Q ≥ R > S
I: T > R ✓
II: S < R ≤ Q < N = K ⇒ S < K ✓
solution.why_others_wrong: Each 'Only' option drops one conclusion that follows along the chain.
solution.final_answer: Option D: Both conclusions I and II are true

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Statement: A ≤ B; B = C; C ≤ D; E > D; F < A; G ≥ E

Conclusions:
I. D > A
II. D = A

options.text: Neither conclusion I nor II is true
Either conclusion I or II is true

solution.concept: Complementary pair along a weak chain
solution.explanation: Combined: F < A ≤ B = C ≤ D < E ≤ G. Only D ≥ A is known, so D > A and D = A are each uncertain, but exactly one of them must be true.
steps: Chain: F < A ≤ B = C ≤ D < E ≤ G
A ≤ D ⇒ D > A or D = A
Either I or II
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Either' replaces 'Both' (four-option rule); neither 'Only' option is certain.
solution.final_answer: Option D: Either conclusion I or II is true

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Here 'A zu B' means 'A is neither smaller than nor equal to B', 'A mi B' means 'A is neither greater than nor equal to B', 'A ro B' means 'A is neither greater than nor smaller than B', 'A te B' means 'A is not smaller than B' and 'A fa B' means 'A is not greater than B'.

Statements: J mi K, K te L, L ro M, M mi N, O fa N, O zu P

Conclusions:
I. J mi N
II. P mi L

options.text: Neither conclusion I nor II is true
Both conclusions I and II are true

solution.concept: Decoding word codes, then reading the chain
solution.explanation: Decoded: J < K ≥ L = M < N ≥ O > P. J and N lie across the turn at K (J < K ≥ L), and P and L lie across the turn at N (M < N ≥ O), so neither conclusion is certain.
steps: Decode: J < K, K ≥ L, L = M, M < N, O ≤ N, O > P
Chain: J < K ≥ L = M < N ≥ O > P
I: reversal at K
II: reversal at N
solution.why_others_wrong: Both conclusions cross a turn in the chain.
solution.final_answer: Option C: Neither conclusion I nor II is true

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: Pointing to a girl, Karan said, "She is the daughter of the only son of my father's mother." How is the girl related to Karan?

solution.concept: Collapse the phrase from the inside out
solution.explanation: Karan's father's mother is his paternal grandmother. Her only son must be Karan's father. The girl is the daughter of Karan's father, so she is Karan's sister.
steps: Father's mother = paternal grandmother
Her only son = Karan's father
Daughter of Karan's father ⇒ sister
solution.why_others_wrong: A cousin would be the child of the father's sibling, but the grandmother has no other son; niece and aunt put the girl in the wrong generation.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: X is the father of Y. Z is the mother of X. W is the only daughter of Z. How is W related to Y?

solution.concept: Father's sister = aunt
solution.explanation: Z is X's mother, and W is Z's daughter, so W is X's sister. X is Y's father, so W is Y's father's sister: Y's aunt.
steps: Z = mother of X; W = daughter of Z ⇒ W is X's sister
X = father of Y ⇒ W = Y's paternal aunt
solution.why_others_wrong: Y's mother is X's wife, not his sister; W is a generation above Y, so not a sister; Z, not W, is Y's grandmother.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: If 'M ki N lo O pa P', how is M related to P?

solution.concept: Decode pair by pair
solution.explanation: M is N's husband; N is O's mother; O is P's brother, so O and P are children of N — and of her husband M. M is P's father.
steps: M ki N: M is N's husband
N lo O and O pa P: O and P are N's children
Children of the couple ⇒ M is the father of P
solution.why_others_wrong: Brother is O's relation to P; Husband is M's relation to N; Uncle would need M to be a sibling of P's parent.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: If 'A su B ne C ki D', how is D related to A?

solution.concept: A parent's brother's wife is an aunt
solution.explanation: A is B's daughter; B is C's sister; C is D's husband. So C is A's maternal uncle, and D, his wife, is A's aunt.
steps: A su B: A is B's daughter
B ne C: C is B's brother ⇒ A's uncle
C ki D: D is C's wife ⇒ A's aunt
solution.why_others_wrong: B, not D, is A's mother; D is B's sister-in-law, not A's; a cousin is in A's own generation.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: Which of the following expressions means that J is the grandmother of K?

options.text: J lo L ki M lo K

solution.concept: Test each option: two generations must separate J and K
solution.explanation: In 'J lo L ki M lo K', J is L's mother, L is M's husband and M is K's mother; so L is K's father and J, L's mother, is K's grandmother. In the other options J is K's sister ('J su L lo K'), aunt ('J ne L lo K') or mother ('J lo L pa K').
steps: J lo L ki M lo K: J → L (son) → K (L is K's father) ⇒ grandmother ✓
J su L lo K ⇒ J is K's sister
J ne L lo K ⇒ J is K's aunt
J lo L pa K ⇒ J is K's mother
solution.why_others_wrong: Each of the other expressions puts J zero or one generation above K.
solution.final_answer: Option C: J lo L ki M lo K

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: If 'E pa F su G ki H', how is H related to E?

solution.concept: The husband's wife is the children's mother
solution.explanation: E is F's brother; F is G's daughter, so E is G's son; G is H's husband, so H is E's mother.
steps: E pa F, F su G ⇒ E and F are G's children
G ki H ⇒ H is G's wife
⇒ H is E's mother
solution.why_others_wrong: F, not H, is E's sister; H is G's wife, not E's; grandmother is one generation too high.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
A family has six members: Om, Pari, Rohan, Shanta, Tushar and Uma, with two married couples.
- Shanta is the mother of Tushar and the mother-in-law of Uma.
- Om is the only grandchild of Shanta, and Om's father is Tushar.
- Pari is the only sister of Tushar.
- Rohan is married to Shanta.

How is Pari related to Uma?

solution.concept: Husband's sister = sister-in-law
solution.explanation: Shanta is Uma's mother-in-law and Tushar's mother; the two couples are Rohan–Shanta and Tushar–Uma, so Uma is Tushar's wife. Pari is Tushar's sister, i.e. Uma's husband's sister: her sister-in-law.
steps: Couples: Rohan–Shanta, Tushar–Uma
Pari = Tushar's sister
Husband's sister ⇒ sister-in-law
solution.why_others_wrong: Pari shares no parent with Uma; Shanta, not Pari, is Uma's mother-in-law; Pari is in Uma's generation, not the next.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: Pointing to a man, Nandini said, "His mother's only daughter is my mother." How is the man related to Nandini?

solution.concept: Identify the shared parent first
solution.explanation: The man's mother's only daughter is the man's sister (his mother has no other daughter). That sister is Nandini's mother, so the man is her mother's brother: her maternal uncle.
steps: His mother's only daughter = his sister
His sister = Nandini's mother
Mother's brother ⇒ maternal uncle
solution.why_others_wrong: Nandini's father is her mother's husband, not her brother; the man is a generation above Nandini; a paternal uncle is the father's brother.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: Vikram is the son-in-law of Leela, who has only one child, Ritu. Vikram and Ritu have only one child, Aarav, and Bina is Aarav's wife. How is Bina related to Vikram?

solution.concept: Son-in-law of a mother of one = husband of that child
solution.explanation: Leela has only one child, Ritu, so her son-in-law Vikram is Ritu's husband. Aarav is their son, and Bina, Aarav's wife, is the wife of Vikram's son: his daughter-in-law.
steps: Leela's only child Ritu ⇒ Vikram is Ritu's husband
Aarav = son of Vikram and Ritu
Wife of one's son ⇒ daughter-in-law
solution.why_others_wrong: Bina is married into the family, so she is not Vikram's daughter; sister-in-law would put her in Vikram's generation; granddaughter puts her two generations below.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability

options.text: K is the mother-in-law of N
O is the father-in-law of M
L is the wife of N
K is the mother of O

solution.concept: Separate what the code fixes from what it leaves open
solution.explanation: K is the mother of L; L is the sister of M, so K is also M's mother; M is N's wife, so K is N's mother-in-law — certain. N is the son of O, so O is M's father-in-law or mother-in-law; O's gender is not given, so 'father-in-law' is not definite. L is N's sister-in-law, not his wife, and K is not O's mother.
steps: K & L, L @ M ⇒ K is M's mother
M % N ⇒ K is N's mother-in-law (definite)
N $ O ⇒ O is a parent of N; O's gender unknown ⇒ 'father-in-law' not definite
solution.why_others_wrong: 'O is the father-in-law of M' fails if O is N's mother; L is N's sister-in-law; K and O are parents of the couple, not mother and child.
solution.final_answer: Option A: K is the mother-in-law of N

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: Anjali cycles 5 km towards the east. She turns left and cycles 3 km, turns left again and cycles 9 km, and then turns left once more and cycles 3 km. How far is she from her starting point, and in which direction?

solution.concept: Track east–west and north–south separately
solution.explanation: East–west: 5 km east, then 9 km west ⇒ 4 km west. North–south: 3 km north (first left from east), then 3 km south (third left) ⇒ 0. She is 4 km west of the start.
steps: Facing east → left = north → left = west → left = south
East–west: +5 − 9 = −4
North–south: +3 − 3 = 0
⇒ 4 km West
solution.why_others_wrong: 4 km East reverses the net east–west movement; 14 km adds the two east–west legs; 3 km North forgets the final 3 km south.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: Early one morning, soon after sunrise, Meera stands in an open field and notices that her shadow falls exactly to her right. She then turns 135° clockwise. In which direction is she facing now?

solution.concept: Morning shadows point west
solution.explanation: In the morning the sun is in the east, so shadows fall to the west. Her shadow is to her right, so her right hand points west and she is facing south. Turning 135° clockwise from south (180°) gives 315°, which is north-west.
steps: Morning sun in the east ⇒ shadow to the west
Right = west ⇒ facing south
South (180°) + 135° clockwise = 315° ⇒ North-West
solution.why_others_wrong: South-West turns only 45°; North-East turns 135° anticlockwise; South-East assumes she first faced north.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: Point B is 10 m east of point A. Point C is 6 m north of point B. Point D is 4 m west of point C. Point E is 11 m south of point D. Point F is 6 m east of point E. What is the shortest distance between A and F, and in which direction is F with respect to A?

solution.concept: Reduce the route to net east and net north displacements
solution.explanation: Take A as the origin. B (10, 0), C (10, 6), D (6, 6), E (6, −5), F (12, −5). F is 12 m east and 5 m south of A, so AF = √(12² + 5²) = √169 = 13 m, towards the south-east.
steps: Net: 12 m east, 5 m south
AF = √(144 + 25) = 13 m, South-East
solution.why_others_wrong: North-East ignores that E is 11 m south of a point only 6 m north of the line AB; 17 m adds the net legs instead of using Pythagoras; 12 m East ignores the 5 m southward offset.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: What is the code for 'clean'?

solution.concept: Strip away the shared words' codes
solution.explanation: city = ri (in all three sentences) and the = mo (shared by sentences 1 and 2). The remaining code of sentence 1 is ka, so clean = ka.
steps: city = ri
the = mo
clean = ka
solution.why_others_wrong: mo is 'the', ri is 'city' and ze is 'sleeps'.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: Which word is coded as 'mo'?

solution.concept: Two shared words: settle one of them from a third sentence
solution.explanation: Sentences 1 and 2 share 'the' and 'city', and the codes 'mo' and 'ri'. Sentence 3 contains 'city' and 'ri' but not 'the' or 'mo', so city = ri and the = mo.
steps: Shared by 1 and 2: the, city ↔ mo, ri
Sentence 3: city = ri
⇒ the = mo
solution.why_others_wrong: city = ri, clean = ka, sleeps = ze.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: Which of the following can be the code for 'glow'?

solution.concept: When two words share two codes, either assignment is possible
solution.explanation: In 'city lights glow' = 'ri pu lo', city = ri, so 'lights' and 'glow' take 'pu' and 'lo' in some order. 'lo' is one of the two possible codes for 'glow'; the others belong to city, sleeps and clean.
steps: city = ri
lights, glow ↔ pu, lo (order unknown)
Among the options only 'lo' is possible
solution.why_others_wrong: ri is 'city', ze is 'sleeps' and ka is 'clean'.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: In a certain code, FLOWER is written as SFXPMG. How is GARDEN written in that code?

solution.concept: Reverse the word, then shift each letter
solution.explanation: FLOWER reversed is REWOLF; moving each letter one place forward gives SFXPMG. GARDEN reversed is NEDRAG; one place forward: OFESBH.
steps: FLOWER → REWOLF → +1 → SFXPMG ✓
GARDEN → NEDRAG → +1 → OFESBH
solution.why_others_wrong: HBSEFO shifts without reversing; OFESBG leaves the last letter unshifted; NDCRZF shifts backward.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: In a certain code, CAT is written as 60 and DOG is written as 28. How is LAMP written in that code?

solution.concept: Only the end letters matter
steps: Code = position of first letter × position of last letter
solution.why_others_wrong: 42 is the sum of all four positions; 28 is the sum of the end positions; 180 multiplies L by O.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: In a certain code, PAINT is written as OCKMS. How is SUGAR written in that code?

solution.concept: Vowels and consonants follow different rules
solution.explanation: In PAINT the vowels A and I move two places forward (C, K) and the consonants P, N and T move one place back (O, M, S). SUGAR: S → R, U → W, G → F, A → C, R → Q, giving RWFCQ.
steps: Vowels +2: A→C, I→K
Consonants −1: P→O, N→M, T→S
SUGAR → R W F C Q
solution.why_others_wrong: RWFCS moves the last R forward; TSHYS reverses both rules; RVFBQ moves the vowels only one place.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: In a certain code language, each word is coded by the same rule, and the codes are written in the same order as the words. 'green leaf' is written as 'N5G F4L', and 'quiet room' is written as 'T5Q M4R'. How is 'deep ocean water' written in that code language?

solution.concept: Code = last letter + length + first letter
solution.explanation: green → last letter N, 5 letters, first letter G: N5G. leaf → F4L; quiet → T5Q; room → M4R. deep → P4D, ocean → N5O, water → R5W.
steps: Pattern: last letter, number of letters, first letter
deep P4D, ocean N5O, water R5W
solution.why_others_wrong: D4P O5N W5R puts the first letter first; P4D N5O R4W miscounts 'water'; P2D N3O R2W counts the vowels instead of the letters.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: What is the code for 'MONEY'?

solution.concept: Watch the wrap-round at the end
solution.explanation: M +2 = O, O −1 = N, N +2 = P, E −1 = D, Y +2 = A (Y → Z → A). MONEY begins with a consonant, so the order is kept: ONPDA.
steps: Odd positions +2: M→O, N→P, Y→A
Even positions −1: O→N, E→D
Starts with M ⇒ no reversal ⇒ ONPDA
solution.why_others_wrong: ONPDW moves Y back instead of forward; ADPNO reverses a word that starts with a consonant; OPPFA moves every letter forward.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: What is the code for 'ASSET'?

solution.concept: Step 2 applies to vowel-initial words
solution.explanation: Step 1: A +2 = C, S −1 = R, S +2 = U, E −1 = D, T +2 = V, giving CRUDV. ASSET begins with a vowel, so step 2 reverses it: VDURC.
steps: Step 1: C R U D V
Starts with A ⇒ reverse ⇒ VDURC
solution.why_others_wrong: CRUDV stops after step 1; VDURE leaves the A unshifted; CTUFV moves every letter forward.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: Which word is coded as 'DNPTU'?

solution.concept: Decode by reversing the two steps
solution.explanation: DNPTU begins with D; if the word started with a vowel the code would be reversed. Undoing step 1 from the left: D −2 = B, N +1 = O, P −2 = N, T +1 = U, U −2 = S: BONUS, which begins with a consonant, so no reversal was applied — consistent.
steps: Undo step 1: −2 on odd positions, +1 on even positions
DNPTU → B O N U S
BONUS starts with a consonant ⇒ no reversal ⇒ consistent
solution.why_others_wrong: BOATS is coded DNCSU, BINGO DHPFQ and BASIS DZUHU.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: In the code for 'EQUITY', which letter is third from the right end?

solution.concept: Apply both steps before counting positions
solution.explanation: Step 1: E→G, Q→P, U→W, I→H, T→V, Y→X, giving GPWHVX. EQUITY begins with a vowel, so the code is XVHWPG. From the right: G, P, W — the third letter is W.
steps: Step 1: G P W H V X
Starts with E ⇒ reverse ⇒ XVHWPG
Third from the right ⇒ W
solution.why_others_wrong: H is third from the right before the reversal; P is second from the right; V is second from the left.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: In a certain code, LOAN is written as 10 and CASH is written as 29. How is SAVE written in that code?

solution.concept: Consonants add, vowels subtract
solution.explanation: Using alphabetical positions, the consonants are added and the vowels subtracted. LOAN: L 12 − O 15 − A 1 + N 14 = 10. CASH: C 3 − A 1 + S 19 + H 8 = 29. SAVE: S 19 − A 1 + V 22 − E 5 = 35.
solution.why_others_wrong: 47 adds all four positions; 41 adds the consonants only; 45 adds E instead of subtracting it.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Study the following arrangement of letters, numbers and symbols and answer the question.

M 4 # R 7 K @ 2 E 9 $ T 5 W & 3 B % 8 H

Which element is 5th to the right of the 11th element from the right end?

solution.concept: Convert a right-end position, then move right
solution.explanation: The 11th element from the right is the 10th from the left (9). Five places to its right is the 15th element from the left: &.
steps: 11th from the right = 20 − 11 + 1 = 10th from the left = 9
solution.why_others_wrong: The other options are the elements one or two places away from the correct position.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Study the following arrangement of letters, numbers and symbols and answer the question.

6 F ★ 3 J A 8 © N 1 S Y £ 5 O 2 G ¥ 4 V

If the first ten elements of the arrangement are written in reverse order, which element will be 4th from the left end?

solution.concept: Reverse a block, then count
solution.explanation: The first ten elements are 6 F ★ 3 J A 8 © N 1; reversed they read 1 N © 8 A J 3 ★ F 6. The 4th from the left is 8 (it was the 7th element from the left, since 10 − 4 + 1 = 7).
steps: Reversed block: 1 N © 8 A J 3 ★ F 6
4th from the left ⇒ original 7th ⇒ 8
solution.why_others_wrong: The other options are the neighbours of the 4th position in the reversed block.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: Count the symbols whose left-hand neighbour is a number. How many such symbols are there?

solution.concept: Look at the left neighbour of every symbol
solution.explanation: The symbols and their left neighbours: 3 *, L !, U #, Q ◆, 9 @, Y ^. Only 3 * and 9 @ have a number before the symbol: two.
steps: Symbols: * ! # ◆ @ ^
Preceded by a number: 3 *, 9 @ ⇒ two

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: What is the sum of the numbers in the arrangement that are immediately followed by a consonant?

solution.concept: Filter by the right neighbour, then add
solution.explanation: Numbers followed by a consonant: 8 L, 6 P, 7 Q, 4 Z, 1 Y. Sum: 8 + 6 + 7 + 4 + 1 = 26. (2 is followed by the vowel U, 3 and 9 by symbols.)
steps: Numbers followed by a consonant: 8, 6, 7, 4, 1
solution.why_others_wrong: 22 leaves out 4; 28 also adds 2, which is followed by the vowel U; 35 also adds 9, which is followed by a symbol.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: Take the stretch of the arrangement that runs from the 3rd element from the left end to the 6th element from the right end. Which element sits at the exact centre of that stretch?

solution.concept: Midway = average of the two positions
solution.explanation: The 3rd from the left is * (position 3). The 6th from the right is position 24 − 6 + 1 = 19 (9). Midway: (3 + 19) ÷ 2 = 11th: U.
steps: 3rd from the left = position 3 (*)
6th from the right = position 19 (9)

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: If the elements are taken in groups of four from the left (D 3 * K, 8 L ! 6, and so on) and the order of the elements within each group is reversed, which element will be 10th from the right end?

solution.concept: Reverse within groups; positions of whole groups do not change
solution.explanation: New arrangement: K * 3 D 6 ! L 8 # U 2 P A ◆ Q 7 @ 9 Z 4 ^ Y 1 G. The 10th from the right is the 15th from the left: Q.
steps: Groups reversed: K * 3 D | 6 ! L 8 | # U 2 P | A ◆ Q 7 | @ 9 Z 4 | ^ Y 1 G
10th from the right = 24 − 10 + 1 = 15th from the left ⇒ Q

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: If all the numbers are removed from the arrangement, which element will be 6th to the left of the 15th element from the left end?

II + III: not sufficient

Both I and II are implicit

solution.explanation: Switching statements to e-mail makes sense only if customers can receive e-mail (I). The decision does not depend on the post having stopped working; banks move to e-mail for cost and speed, so II is not assumed.
steps: E-mail statements ⇒ customers can receive e-mail: I implicit
No need for the post to have stopped: II not implicit
solution.why_others_wrong: Only II and Both accept a claim the decision does not rely on; Neither ignores the basis of the change.
solution.final_answer: Option A: Only assumption I is implicit

options.text: Neither I nor II is implicit
Both I and II are implicit

steps: Extension ⇒ some had not paid ⇒ I contradicts the statement
A further extension is not implied ⇒ II not implicit

Conclusions:

options.text: Neither conclusion I nor II follows
Both conclusions I and II follow

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability

Below are two statements, I and II. They may be independent causes, effects of independent causes or of a common cause, or one may be the effect of the other. Decide the relationship.

II. The market road was under knee-deep water for several hours on Tuesday.

options.text: Statement I is the cause and statement II is its effect
Statement II is the cause and statement I is its effect
Both the statements I and II are effects of independent causes
Both the statements I and II are effects of some common cause

solution.concept: Cause and effect: look for a direct link, a shared trigger, or none
solution.explanation: Water escaping from a burst pipeline under the road floods the road. I directly explains II, and the timing matches.
steps: I: pipeline under the road bursts
II: the same road floods the same day
I → II

II. Students had asked the college for a quiet place to study in the evenings during the examination month, since their hostels have no study rooms.

options.text: Statement I is the cause and statement II is its effect
Statement II is the cause and statement I is its effect
Both the statements I and II are effects of independent causes
Both the statements I and II are effects of some common cause

solution.concept: Cause and effect: look for a direct link, a shared trigger, or none
solution.explanation: The students' request for an evening study place is the reason the library stays open later. II is the cause and I its effect.
steps: II: demand for an evening study place
I: library opens till 10 pm
II → I

solution.final_answer: Option B: Statement II is the cause and statement I is its effect

questions.question_text:

II. Hospitals in the district set up special wards for heatstroke patients this week.

options.text: Statement I is the cause and statement II is its effect
Statement II is the cause and statement I is its effect
Both the statements I and II are effects of independent causes
Both the statements I and II are effects of some common cause

solution.concept: Cause and effect: look for a direct link, a shared trigger, or none
solution.explanation: Earlier school closing does not make hospitals open heatstroke wards, and heatstroke wards do not change school timings. Both are typical responses to one event — a severe heatwave in the district this week.
steps: No direct link between the two
Both are standard responses to extreme heat
⇒ effects of a common cause
solution.why_others_wrong: Effects of independent causes would need two unrelated reasons in the same week; one heatwave explains both.
solution.final_answer: Option D: Both the statements I and II are effects of some common cause

II. A private bank launched a new credit card for college students.

options.text: Statement I is the cause and statement II is its effect
Statement II is the cause and statement I is its effect
Both the statements I and II are effects of independent causes
Both the statements I and II are effects of some common cause

solution.concept: Cause and effect: look for a direct link, a shared trigger, or none
solution.explanation: Repainting road markings follows from the corporation's road-safety work; a new card follows from a bank's business plans. Neither explains the other, and no single event explains both.
steps: I: outcome of civic road maintenance
II: outcome of a bank's product decision
⇒ independent causes

I. The central bank sharply lowered, with immediate effect, the maximum amount that any one bank may lend to a single borrower.
II. Several large companies that had been borrowing heavily from a single bank began spreading their borrowing across many banks.

options.text: Statement I is the cause and statement II is its effect
Statement II is the cause and statement I is its effect
Both the statements I and II are effects of independent causes
Both the statements I and II are effects of some common cause

solution.concept: Cause and effect: look for a direct link, a shared trigger, or none
solution.explanation: Once one bank may lend a large borrower only a smaller amount, a company that needs the same total credit must go to several banks. The new limit (I) directly explains the companies' change (II).
steps: I: a lower single-borrower limit for each bank
II: big borrowers split loans across banks
Limit forces the split ⇒ I is the cause
solution.why_others_wrong: Companies spreading their loans cannot have caused a regulator's limit that took effect immediately before it, so B fails; no outside event is needed.
solution.final_answer: Option A: Statement I is the cause and statement II is its effect

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Below are two statements, I and II. They may be independent causes, effects of independent causes or of a common cause, or one may be the effect of the other. Decide the relationship.

II. Sugarcane output in the state fell by a third this year because of a severe drought.

options.text: Statement I is the cause and statement II is its effect
Statement II is the cause and statement I is its effect
Both the statements I and II are effects of independent causes
Both the statements I and II are effects of some common cause

solution.concept: Cause and effect: look for a direct link, a shared trigger, or none
solution.explanation: Mills crush the cane that farmers supply; with a third less cane, they run out of cane and close the season early. The drought-hit output (II) explains the early end (I).
steps: II: one-third less cane, caused by drought
I: mills stop crushing a month early
Less cane → shorter season ⇒ II is the cause
solution.why_others_wrong: An early end to crushing cannot reduce the cane grown in a drought year, so A fails; the drought is already part of II, so no separate common cause is needed.
solution.final_answer: Option B: Statement II is the cause and statement I is its effect

II. Shops in the state's markets reported record sales of clothes and sweets in the week before Diwali.

options.text: Statement I is the cause and statement II is its effect
Statement II is the cause and statement I is its effect
Both the statements I and II are effects of independent causes
Both the statements I and II are effects of some common cause

solution.concept: Cause and effect: look for a direct link, a shared trigger, or none
solution.explanation: People withdraw cash and shop heavily for the same reason — festival buying before Diwali. Cash withdrawals do not by themselves create sales (people could withdraw and not spend), and shop sales do not cause withdrawals; both follow from the festival season.
steps: No direct cause: withdrawals ≠ purchases
Both are typical of pre-festival spending
⇒ effects of a common cause
solution.why_others_wrong: A or B would need one statement to produce the other; D would need two unrelated reasons, though both are tied to the same festival week.
solution.final_answer: Option D: Both the statements I and II are effects of some common cause

Both the statements I and II are effects of some common cause

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability

The branch should get the water cooler repaired or replaced without delay
The branch should stop elderly customers from waiting inside
The branch should remove the water cooler permanently

steps: Problem: no working water cooler
Remedy: repair or replace it

Students with back pain should be asked to stay at home
Schools should set a daily timetable so that students carry only the books needed that day, and provide lockers for the rest

solution.concept: Practical, targeted remedy
solution.explanation: Carrying only the day's books and keeping the rest in lockers lightens the bags directly, without harming studies.

Remedy: day-wise books + lockers

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability

Passage: The town's only bridge across the river will be closed for repairs from 1 March to 15 March. During this period a ferry will carry people across the river every 30 minutes from 6 am to 9 pm. There is no other way to cross the river near the town.

Which of the following can be inferred from the passage?

options.text: During the closure, a person in the town who needs to cross the river at 11 pm will not be able to do so
The ferry will continue to run after the bridge reopens
The repairs will be completed before 15 March
Most people in the town cross the river every day

solution.explanation: Between 1 and 15 March the bridge is closed, the ferry runs only from 6 am to 9 pm, and there is no other way to cross. So at 11 pm nobody can cross.
steps: Bridge closed; ferry 6 am–9 pm; no other crossing
11 pm is outside ferry hours ⇒ cannot cross
solution.why_others_wrong: The passage says nothing about the ferry after the closure, early completion, or how many people cross daily.

Speed breakers are cheap to build
Some students come to school by bus

solution.explanation: Speed breakers slow vehicles. If the accidents near the gate were mostly caused by fast vehicles, slowing them should reduce accidents.
steps: Remedy: slower vehicles
Strengthener: accidents were speed-related

The 8:15 am bus stops at the district hospital
The 8:15 am bus is always crowded
No bus on any other route stops at the district hospital

solution.explanation: All route-7 buses stop at the hospital, and the 8:15 am bus is a route-7 bus, so it stops at the hospital.
steps: All route 7 buses → hospital
8:15 am bus ∈ route 7 ⇒ stops at hospital

questions.question_text:
Statement: In a village, many wells have dried up because groundwater is being pumped out faster than rainwater can refill it.

Which of the following is the most appropriate course of action?

options.text: Dig all the existing wells deeper
Ask the villagers to leave the village
Encourage rainwater harvesting and regulate the digging of new borewells in the village
Ban the use of water for all farming

solution.concept: Address both sides of the imbalance
solution.explanation: The wells dry because withdrawal exceeds recharge. Rainwater harvesting adds recharge and regulating borewells limits withdrawal, so both sides of the imbalance are addressed.
steps: Cause: pumping > recharge
Remedy: more recharge, controlled pumping
solution.why_others_wrong: Deeper wells speed up depletion; moving villagers away or banning all farming is impractical and extreme.
solution.final_answer: Option C: Encourage rainwater harvesting and regulate the digging of new borewells in the village

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Argument: The new online examination portal is more reliable than the old one, because complaints about the portal crashing on exam day fell from 40 last year to 5 this year.

Which of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the argument?

options.text: The new portal has a more attractive design
The new portal was built by a well-known company
Some candidates did not know how to file a complaint
About 40,000 candidates used the portal last year, but only about 3,000 used it this year

solution.concept: Weaken: compare rates, not raw counts
solution.explanation: 40 complaints from 40,000 users is 0.1%; 5 from 3,000 users is about 0.17%. The complaint rate actually rose, so the fall in the number of complaints does not show greater reliability.
steps: Rate rose ⇒ evidence fails
solution.why_others_wrong: Design and the builder's reputation say nothing about crashes; not knowing how to complain applies to both years and does not explain the change.
solution.final_answer: Option D: About 40,000 candidates used the portal last year, but only about 3,000 used it this year

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
